title: Pickleball after 60 in New Jersey: how to get started
dek: The paddle sport filling New Jersey's park courts is easy to learn, cheap to try and very social. Here is how to find a game, what to buy and how to avoid the common injuries.
keyFacts: 24.3 million Americans played pickleball in 2025 (SFIA).
Find courts and beginner sessions through your town recreation department, county parks, YMCA or senior center.
Players 50+ accounted for 91% of ER-treated pickleball injuries in a 2013 to 2022 study.
Eye doctors recommend polycarbonate goggles with front and side coverage.
body:
Walk past almost any town park in New Jersey on a weekday morning and you will hear it: the hollow pop of a plastic ball on a paddle, followed by laughter. Pickleball has become one of the easiest ways for people over 60 to get moving, meet neighbors and enjoy a little friendly competition. This guide covers what it costs, what to buy, where to find a game near you and how to stay safe while you learn.

Why are so many older adults playing pickleball?

Pickleball is a paddle sport played on a court about a third the size of a tennis court. Most people play doubles, so you cover less ground than you would in tennis. The ball is light plastic with holes, and it moves slower than a tennis ball. Rallies start quickly, even for beginners.

The sport has grown fast. The Sports and Fitness Industry Association (SFIA) counted 24.3 million American players in 2025, up from about 4.2 million in 2020. The American Academy of Ophthalmology notes that the game is especially popular with people 65 and older.

Players give a few reasons for sticking with it:

  • It is social. Doubles means four people on a court, and open play groups rotate partners, so you meet new people every session.
  • It is quick to learn. Most newcomers can keep a short rally going after a lesson or two.
  • It scales to your fitness. You can play a gentle game of soft shots at the net or a brisk game with more running.
  • It is close to home. Many New Jersey towns have painted pickleball lines on tennis courts or built dedicated courts in local parks.
Most beginners can keep a short rally going after a lesson or two.

What does it cost to start?

Pickleball is one of the cheaper sports to try. Many town and county courts are free to use on a first come, first served basis. Some towns charge a small seasonal fee or require a resident permit, so check your recreation department before you go.

Here is what you might pay for:

  • A paddle and balls. You do not need a premium paddle to start. Many recreation programs and clinics lend paddles to first timers, which lets you try the game before you buy.
  • Court shoes. This is the one item worth spending on. More on that below.
  • Lessons or clinics. Town recreation programs, YMCAs and senior centers often run low cost beginner sessions. Ask whether there is a senior rate.
  • Indoor court time. In winter, look for indoor play at YMCAs, town community centers and school gyms used by recreation departments. Fees vary, so ask about weekday daytime sessions, which are often cheaper and less crowded.

What equipment do I need?

The gear list is short. Here is what to bring to your first session.

Paddle

Paddles are solid, with no strings, and are usually made of composite or graphite. A midweight paddle is a sensible start for most people. If you have elbow or shoulder trouble, ask an instructor to let you try a few weights before you buy.

Balls

Outdoor balls are harder and have smaller holes to cut through wind. Indoor balls are softer with larger holes. Buy the type that matches where you will play most.

Shoes

Wear court shoes made for tennis or pickleball. They support side to side movement. Running shoes are built for forward motion and can make it easier to roll an ankle when you shuffle sideways.

Eye protection

Protective eyewear is not required, but eye doctors recommend it. See the safety section below.

Court basicsMeasurement
Court size20 feet wide by 44 feet long
Non-volley zone ("the kitchen")7 feet deep on each side of the net
Net height at the sidelines36 inches
Net height at the center34 inches

Where can I find courts and beginner sessions in New Jersey?

Court schedules change by season, and many towns post open play times only on their own websites or bulletin boards. These are the most reliable places to look.

  1. Start with your town recreation department. Search your town's name plus "recreation pickleball," or call the rec office. Ask about open play hours, beginner clinics, resident fees and whether courts are shared with tennis.
  2. Check your county parks department. Several New Jersey county park systems have pickleball courts and run seasonal programs. Your county's parks and recreation website will list locations and any reservation rules.
  3. Ask your local senior center. Many senior centers organize pickleball groups or carpools to nearby courts. Your county Office on Aging can point you to one. Call the statewide Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 to reach yours.
  4. Call a nearby YMCA. Many Ys offer indoor pickleball, beginner clinics and drop in play. Membership rules differ by location, and some Ys offer financial assistance.
  5. Plan for winter. Outdoor play in New Jersey slows from late fall to early spring. Ask your recreation department, county parks office and YMCA about indoor sessions in gyms and community centers, and whether they hold beginner hours.
  6. Ask people at the courts. Regular players know when the friendliest beginner groups meet. A short chat at a town park on a weekday morning often tells you more than any website.
Tip for your first visit

Arrive a few minutes early and tell the group you are new. Open play groups are used to beginners, and someone will usually explain how paddles are stacked to rotate players onto the courts.

How do I stay safe on the court?

Pickleball is gentler than many sports, but injuries do happen, and they happen most often to older players. A study published in 2025 in the Journal of the American Osteopathic Academy of Orthopedics reviewed emergency room data from 2013 to 2022. Players 50 and older made up 91% of pickleball injuries in that study. Fractures and sprains were the most common injuries, each about 27% of the total, and the trunk and wrist were among the areas hurt most often. Falling onto an outstretched hand is a common way to break a wrist.

Eye injuries are rising too. A 2025 study in JAMA Ophthalmology found that 70% of pickleball eye injuries treated in emergency rooms involved players 50 or older.

Simple habits that lower your risk

  • Warm up for 5 to 10 minutes. Walk, do gentle arm circles and leg swings, and hit easy shots at the net before you play points.
  • Never back up to chase a lob. Backpedaling is a classic cause of falls. Turn sideways and shuffle, or let the ball go.
  • Wear eye protection. The American Academy of Ophthalmology says polycarbonate safety goggles with front and side coverage are the ideal choice. Even sunglasses or regular glasses are better than nothing.
  • Wear court shoes and replace them when the tread wears smooth.
  • Drink water and take breaks, especially on hot summer courts.
  • Pace yourself. Start with an hour or two a week and build up.
  • Talk to your doctor first if you have heart disease, balance problems, osteoporosis or a recent joint replacement.
When to get help right away

After a ball to the eye, see an eye doctor right away if you notice vision changes, real pain, bleeding or bruising. For a fall with wrist pain or swelling, get it checked. Wrist fractures are easy to mistake for sprains.

For more ways to stay active, see our guide to healthy aging in New Jersey.

What should I know about etiquette and skill ratings?

Pickleball has a friendly culture, and a few unwritten rules help you fit in fast.

  • Follow the paddle rotation. At busy courts, players stack paddles in a rack or line. When a game ends, the next group goes on.
  • Call the score before you serve. In doubles, the server calls three numbers: their team's score, the other team's score and whether they are the first or second server.
  • Make line calls on your side honestly. If you are not sure, the ball is in.
  • Do not walk behind a court during a rally. Wait for the point to end.
  • Learn the kitchen rule. You cannot hit the ball out of the air while standing in the non-volley zone.
  • Thank your partner and opponents with a paddle tap at the net after each game.

What do the skill numbers mean?

Groups often organize play by skill level. Most use a self-rating scale that runs from about 1.0 for brand new players to 5.0 and above for experts.

LevelWhat it usually means
1.0Brand new, still learning the basic rules
2.0 to 2.5Beginner who can sustain a short rally and keep score
3.0Advanced beginner with medium paced shots, still inconsistent
3.5Intermediate
4.0 and upAdvanced players

You can rate yourself at the start. Be modest. Playing in a group slightly below your level feels better than struggling in one above it.

faq.q: Am I too old to start pickleball at 70?
faq.a: Many people start in their 70s and beyond. Begin with a beginner clinic, play for short sessions and check with your doctor first if you have heart, balance or bone health concerns.

faq.q: Do I need to buy a paddle before my first lesson?
faq.a: Usually not. Many town recreation programs, senior centers and YMCAs lend paddles to beginners. Ask when you sign up.

faq.q: How do I find pickleball courts near me in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call your town recreation department or county parks department, ask your local senior center, or check with a nearby YMCA. The ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 can connect you to your county office on aging, which often knows where senior groups play.

faq.q: Is eye protection required?
faq.a: No, but the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends it. Polycarbonate safety goggles with front and side coverage offer the best protection.

faq.q: Where can I play pickleball indoors in New Jersey in winter?
faq.a: Ask your town recreation department, county parks office and local YMCA about indoor sessions in gyms and community centers. Many run weekday daytime play that suits retirees, and some senior centers organize groups.

sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology: Pickleball eye protection
Review of Optometry: JAMA Ophthalmology study on pickleball eye injuries
AOAO: Rising orthopedic injuries in pickleball (10-year national study)
seoDesc: Pickleball after 60 in New Jersey: how to find a game on park courts, what to buy and how to avoid common injuries.

title: Working after 60 in New Jersey: jobs, training and your rights
dek: Part-time work, paid training through SCSEP or a second career can all make sense after 60. Here is where to find help in New Jersey and how a paycheck affects Social Security, Medicare and taxes.
keyFacts: 2027 Social Security earnings limit under full retirement age: $25,560.
SCSEP: age 55+, unemployed, family income up to 125% of the poverty level.
NJ Division on Civil Rights: 1-833-653-2748; file within 180 days.
NJ minimum wage: $15.92 an hour for most workers in 2026.
SCORE and the NJ SBDC offer free small business help.
body:
Plenty of New Jerseyans keep working after 60. Some need the income. Others want structure, purpose or a reason to get out of the house. Whatever your reason, a paycheck after 60 comes with its own rules on Social Security, Medicare and taxes. This guide walks through job ideas, free training programs, your legal rights and the money questions to settle before you say yes to an offer.

What kinds of work fit well after 60?

The best fit is usually work that uses skills you already have, on a schedule you control. A few ideas that suit New Jersey well:

  • Seasonal Shore jobs. Beach towns hire for summer in retail, hospitality, beach badge checking and visitor services. Start asking in early spring.
  • Holiday retail and warehouse work. Stores and distribution centers hire extra help from October through December.
  • Poll worker. New Jersey pays poll workers $300 for Election Day and $21.43 an hour on in-person early voting days. You must be a registered voter in your county. Apply through the New Jersey Division of Elections or call 609-292-3760.
  • Substitute teaching. New Jersey's substitute credential requires 30 college credits, a sponsoring district, a criminal history check and a $125 application fee, according to the NJ Department of Education.
  • Tutoring, coaching and library or museum work. Retired teachers, accountants and tradespeople are often in demand for part-time roles.
  • Consulting for your old field. Former employers sometimes bring retirees back on contract for busy seasons or special projects.
  • Caregiving and companion work. Home care agencies hire companions and aides. Some roles need training or certification.

New Jersey's minimum wage rose to $15.92 an hour for most employees on January 1, 2026. Seasonal and small employers pay at least $15.23.

Watch for job scams

Be wary of work from home offers that ask you to pay for training, deposit checks or buy gift cards. Real employers do not charge you to start. See our guide to scams targeting New Jersey seniors.

What is SCSEP, and who runs it in New Jersey?

The Senior Community Service Employment Program (SCSEP) is a federal program that pays older, low income job seekers to train in part-time community service jobs. Participants work at nonprofits and public agencies while they build skills and look for a regular job.

Who qualifies?

According to the New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development (NJDOL), you must be:

  • At least 55 years old
  • Unemployed
  • Living on family income no higher than 125% of the federal poverty level

Priority goes to people 65 and older, veterans and eligible spouses, people with disabilities, people with limited English or low literacy, rural residents, and people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness, among others. NJDOL says participants train an average of 18 hours a week and are paid minimum wage.

Who runs it here?

In New Jersey, SCSEP is offered by several organizations:

  • NJDOL's WorkForce 55+ program runs SCSEP through One-Stop Career Centers in many counties, including Atlantic, Camden, Cape May, Cumberland, Essex, Gloucester, Hudson, Hunterdon, Middlesex, Monmouth, Sussex and Union. County phone numbers are on the WorkForce 55+ page.
  • Easterseals New Jersey also runs a SCSEP program, based in East Brunswick. Ask your county WorkForce 55+ office which provider covers your town.
  • PathStone runs a SCSEP office in Vineland.

The AARP Foundation runs SCSEP in many states, but its office locator did not list any New Jersey sites when we checked. Its Work Resources Helpline, 1-855-850-2525, can tell you which provider serves your area.

Funding is uncertain

The U.S. Department of Labor's budget request for fiscal year 2027 again proposes eliminating the program, and Congress has not settled the issue. Call a local provider to confirm openings before you count on a slot.

Where can I get free job search help?

New Jersey's public job centers are called One-Stop Career Centers. You may also see them called American Job Centers, the federal name for the same network. They are free and open to job seekers of any age.

Staff can help you with:

  • Updating a resume that may list decades of experience
  • Learning job search websites and online applications
  • Free online skills courses
  • Training grants, if you qualify
  • Older worker services and referrals to SCSEP

Find your nearest center and request an appointment through NJDOL Career Services. Your public library is another good stop. Many New Jersey libraries offer free computer help and resume workshops. See our guide to learning something new for classes that can refresh your skills.

What are my rights if I face age bias?

Two laws protect older workers in New Jersey.

The federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA)

The ADEA protects workers and job applicants who are 40 or older. It applies to employers with 20 or more employees. It covers hiring, firing, pay, promotions, training and layoffs. You generally have 180 days to file a charge with the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), and state law can extend that window.

The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD)

The LAD also bans age discrimination at work, and it reaches many employers too small for the federal law. Until 2021, the LAD let employers refuse to hire or promote people over 70. A law signed on October 5, 2021, removed that exception, so workers over 70 now have the same protection as everyone else.

You can file a complaint with the New Jersey Division on Civil Rights within 180 days of what happened. Call 1-833-653-2748 (1-833-NJDCR4U) or file online. You can also go to Superior Court within two years, but you cannot pursue both at the same time.

Keep a record

If you suspect age bias, write down dates, what was said and who was there. Save emails, texts and job postings. These details help an investigator or lawyer.

How do earnings affect Social Security before full retirement age?

If you collect Social Security before your full retirement age and keep working, the Social Security Administration (SSA) may hold back some benefits. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. This is called the earnings test.

Your situation in 2027Earnings limitWhat SSA withholds
Under full retirement age all year$25,560$1 for every $2 above the limit
Reaching full retirement age in 2027$67,920$1 for every $3 above the limit, counting only earnings before the month you reach full retirement age
At or past full retirement ageNo limitNothing

Say you are 63, living in Cherry Hill, and collecting $1,500 a month. You take a job paying $35,560 in 2027. That is $10,000 over the limit, so SSA would withhold $5,000 of your benefits for the year. SSA usually does this by holding back full monthly payments until the amount is covered.

That money is not gone for good. Once you reach full retirement age, SSA recalculates your monthly benefit to credit the months it held back. Report your expected earnings to SSA so you are not hit with an overpayment notice later. Call 1-800-772-1213 or use your my Social Security account.

Benefits are rising 3.6% in January 2027. Read more in our Social Security 2027 guide.

Medicare and taxes: what changes when you keep working?

Medicare

If you work past 65 and have health coverage through your job, your employer's size matters.

  • 20 or more employees: You can usually delay Part B without a penalty. You get an 8-month Special Enrollment Period after you or your spouse stop working or the coverage ends.
  • Fewer than 20 employees: Medicare usually pays first. Your job coverage may not pay for services unless you have both Part A and Part B. Sign up on time.

The Part B premium is $202.90 a month in 2026. Before you decide, call New Jersey's free State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820. Our turning 65 guide covers enrollment step by step.

Taxes

  • Federal tax on Social Security. Wages can push more of your benefit into taxable income. Benefits may be taxed if your combined income is above $25,000 for individuals or $32,000 for joint filers.
  • New senior deduction. For tax years 2025 through 2028, people 65 and older can take an extra $6,000 federal deduction ($12,000 for a couple if both qualify). It shrinks for incomes above $75,000, or $150,000 for joint filers.
  • New Jersey income tax. New Jersey does not tax Social Security benefits. Your wages are taxable, and working can affect some state retirement income exclusions. Check the NJ Division of Taxation's retirement guide or ask a tax preparer.
  • Property tax relief. Earned income counts toward the income limits for Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ. See our property tax relief guide.
A part-time paycheck can change your taxes, your Medicare timing and your property tax relief. Check all three before you start.

Thinking about starting a small business?

Many people turn a lifetime of skills into a consulting practice, a craft business or a small service company. Two free resources can help New Jersey residents get started.

  • SCORE New Jersey. SCORE pairs you with a volunteer business mentor, free for the life of your business. SCORE has six chapters serving New Jersey. Request a mentor at score.org/nj or call 1-800-634-0245.
  • America's SBDC New Jersey. The New Jersey Small Business Development Center network offers no-cost, one-on-one consulting, with its state office at Rutgers Business School in Newark. Visit njsbdc.com or call 973-353-1927.

Before you launch, ask a mentor about business registration, self-employment tax and how business income counts toward the Social Security earnings test.

faq.q: How much can I earn in 2027 without losing Social Security benefits?
faq.a: If you are under full retirement age all year, SSA withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $25,560. In the year you reach full retirement age, it withholds $1 for every $3 above $67,920, counting only earnings before that month. After full retirement age there is no limit.

faq.q: Does AARP run SCSEP in New Jersey?
faq.a: AARP Foundation's locator did not list New Jersey offices when we checked. In New Jersey, SCSEP is offered by NJDOL's WorkForce 55+ program through One-Stop Career Centers, Easterseals New Jersey and PathStone in Vineland. AARP Foundation's helpline at 1-855-850-2525 can point you to a provider.

faq.q: Can an employer refuse to hire me because I am over 70?
faq.a: No. A 2021 change to the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination removed the exception that once allowed employers to refuse to hire or promote people over 70.

faq.q: Do I need Medicare Part B if I am still working?
faq.a: If your employer has 20 or more employees and you have group coverage through the job, you can usually delay Part B without penalty. If the employer has fewer than 20, Medicare usually pays first, so you generally need Parts A and B. Call SHIP at 1-800-792-8820 for free advice.

faq.q: Where can I get free help with a job search?
faq.a: New Jersey's One-Stop Career Centers, also called American Job Centers, offer free resume help, workshops and training referrals. Start at nj.gov/labor/career-services.

faq.q: How much do New Jersey poll workers get paid?
faq.a: New Jersey pays poll workers $300 for Election Day and $21.43 an hour on in-person early voting days. You must be a U.S. citizen, a New Jersey resident and a registered voter in your county.

title: Golf for seniors in New Jersey: county courses and discounts
dek: County golf courses across New Jersey sell senior cards that cut the price of every round. Here is what they cost, where to play a shorter round and how to stay comfortable on the course.
keyFacts: Most county park systems sell a yearly senior golf card that lowers greens fees.
Senior age is 62+ in Essex, Union, Bergen, Somerset and Ocean, and 65+ in Morris and Monmouth.
Nine-hole, par 3 and executive courses make for a shorter, cheaper round.
The CDC counts golf while walking and carrying clubs as moderate activity.
body:
Golf is one of the easiest sports to keep playing for decades. You set the pace, you can walk or ride, and a round with friends fills a whole morning. New Jersey makes it affordable, too: most county park systems run public courses and sell a senior golf card that cuts the price of every round. This guide explains how those cards work, where to find shorter courses and how to play comfortably in the heat.

How do county senior golf discounts work?

Almost every county uses the same system. You buy a yearly golf ID card in person at one of the county courses, bringing proof of age and proof that you live in the county. Once you have the card, you pay the lower senior greens fee each time you play, and in several counties you can book tee times further ahead than people without a card. Some senior rates apply only on weekdays or in the morning.

The age that counts as "senior" depends on the county. Essex, Union, Bergen, Somerset and Ocean start at 62. Morris and Monmouth start at 65. Some counties don't state an age online, so call the golf shop before you go.

What do the county senior cards cost in 2026?

These are the 2026 prices posted on official county golf sites. Fees can change during the season, so confirm with the course.

CountyCoursesSenior card (residents)
BergenDarlington, Orchard Hills, Overpeck, Rockleigh, Soldier Hill, Valley Brook$45 registration, age 62+ (as of December 31). Senior weekday greens fee $28 for 18 holes
EssexFrancis A. Byrne, Hendricks Field, Weequahic$49 Golf ID, age 62+. Senior weekday fee with the card: $35 at Weequahic and Hendricks Field, $45 at Francis Byrne
MonmouthBel-Aire, Charleston Springs, Hominy Hill, Howell Park, Pine Brook, Shark RiverResident Senior Golf Pass, age 65+: $52 for one year or $89 for two
MorrisFlanders Valley, Sunset Valley, Pinch Brook, Berkshire Valley$27 registration card, age 65+, gives resident rates
OceanAtlantis, Forge Pond$30 resident Golf ID. Senior morning rate (62+): $19 at Atlantis, $14 at Forge Pond
SomersetNeshanic Valley, Green Knoll, Spooky Brook, Quail Brook$70 resident senior ID, age 62+
UnionGalloping Hill, Ash Brook$35 Player's Card for senior residents 62+

Middlesex (Tamarack, The Meadows at Middlesex, Raritan Landing) sells a $45 resident Advantage Card with senior rates, Mercer (Mercer Oaks, Mountain View, Princeton Country Club, Hopewell Valley) offers a lower junior and senior member rate, Passaic runs Preakness Valley in Wayne, and Hudson's nine-hole Skyway course in Jersey City has a weekday senior rate for golfers 62 and over. Check each course's rates page for current prices.

Where can I play a shorter round?

Eighteen holes on a full-length course can take more than four hours. Shorter courses are cheaper, quicker and easier on the back, and several county systems have them:

  • Nine-hole courses: Orchard Hills in Paramus and the Blue nine at Rockleigh (Bergen), Skyway in Jersey City (Hudson), and the Academy Course at Neshanic Valley (Somerset), which the county describes as perfect for walking.
  • Par 3 and pitch and putt: the nine-hole par 3 at Bel-Aire (Monmouth), the par 27 pitch and putt at Ash Brook (Union) and at Green Knoll (Somerset), and the nine-hole practice course at the Galloping Hill Learning Center (Union).
  • Executive courses: Pinch Brook (Morris, par 65), Forge Pond (Ocean, par 60) and Raritan Landing (Middlesex, par 58 with 14 par 3s).

Should I move up to the forward tees?

Yes, if your drives have gotten shorter. USGA research found that a forward tee closer to 4,000 yards than 5,000 suits far more players, and the "Tee It Forward" idea from the PGA of America and the USGA suggests about 3,500 to 3,700 yards for someone who drives the ball about 140 yards. Playing the right tees makes the game more fun and speeds up play. The USGA has a free online course length calculator that suggests a tee based on how far you hit a 7-iron.

Is golf good exercise after 60?

It can be. The CDC lists golf while walking and carrying your clubs as moderate-intensity activity, the kind that counts toward the 150 minutes a week it recommends for adults 65 and older. The CDC also recommends muscle-strengthening activity at least two days a week and activities that improve balance. Riding in a cart is still a good way to get outside and stay social on days when walking the whole course is too much.

How do I stay safe in the heat and sun?

  • Play early. Book a morning tee time on hot days. The CDC notes UV rays are strongest between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.
  • Drink before you're thirsty. The CDC says adults 65 and older are more prone to heat illness and should drink more water than usual.
  • Dress for it. Wear loose, light-colored clothing, a brimmed hat and sunglasses that block UV.
  • Use sunscreen. Choose broad-spectrum SPF 15 or higher and reapply after two hours or after sweating.

Are there senior golf leagues?

Some counties run them. The Monmouth County Park System has a Men's 60+ Touring League that plays at four county courses (spring sign-ups through the park system, 732-842-4000, extension 1). Mercer County golf lists a senior citizens golf association for county residents 60 and older, with outings from April to October. In other counties, ask your town recreation department or senior center whether a group meets at the local course.

What if I have a disability?

Several counties offer help. Essex and Bergen sell discounted golf cards to golfers with a qualifying disability, Monmouth issues free permits for a player assistant on the day of play, and Middlesex says it will make reasonable accommodations if you contact the golf staff.

faq.q: At what age do I get a senior golf rate in New Jersey?
faq.a: It depends on the county. Essex, Union, Bergen, Somerset and Ocean use 62, and Morris and Monmouth use 65. Ask the golf shop if the county site doesn't say.

faq.q: Do I need to live in the county to get the senior rate?
faq.a: The lowest rates are for county residents with a golf ID card. Some counties sell cards to nonresidents at a higher price.

faq.q: Where can I play a quick round?
faq.a: Try a nine-hole, par 3 or executive course, such as Orchard Hills in Paramus, Bel-Aire in Monmouth, the Academy Course at Neshanic Valley or Pinch Brook in Morris County.

faq.q: Does golf count as exercise?
faq.a: Yes. The CDC lists golf while walking and carrying clubs as moderate-intensity activity, which counts toward the 150 minutes a week recommended for older adults.

title: Activities for homebound seniors in New Jersey
dek: Can't get out much? Books by mail, friendly callers, online classes, safe exercise and rides for the odd outing can keep life full. Here is what New Jersey offers.
keyFacts: The NJ State Library's Talking Book and Braille Center mails audiobooks free. Call 1-800-792-8322.
Call 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging for friendly visitor and caller programs.
The CDC says to be as active as your abilities allow. Some activity beats none.
NJ Transit Access Link offers curb to curb rides for people who can't use local buses.
body:
When getting out of the house gets hard, the days can shrink fast. Maybe it is a bad hip, a heart condition, failing eyesight, or simply no car and no easy bus. The good news is that a lot can come to you. Books arrive by mail, volunteers call or visit, classes run on a tablet, and a van can take you out when you want to go.

This guide is for older adults in New Jersey who spend most of their time at home, and for the family members helping them.

Can the library come to me?

Yes, in two ways.

The Talking Book and Braille Center. The New Jersey State Library runs this free service for residents of any age who have trouble reading standard print or holding a book because of a vision problem, a physical limitation or a reading disability. Members can borrow from more than 100,000 titles and 40 magazines in audio and braille. Books come and go by mail as free matter for the blind, so there is no postage to pay, or you can download them through the national BARD service. Registered members can borrow a digital talking book player on a long-term loan at no cost. The application has to be certified to confirm eligibility. Call 1-800-792-8322. The center is open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

The same center runs the Library Equal Access Program, free iPad accessibility courses for adults 55 and older with some vision loss.

Your local or county library. Many New Jersey libraries deliver or mail books to people who cannot get in. A few examples we confirmed:

  • Morris County Library runs Libraries by Mail, a free service for Morris County residents who cannot get to their local library. Return postage is prepaid. Call 973-285-6970.
  • Bloomfield Public Library offers free weekly home delivery to Bloomfield cardholders who are homebound, for a short time or for good. Call 973-566-6200.
  • Ocean City Free Public Library brings items to the front door of homebound Ocean City residents every two weeks.
  • Burlington County Library mails books, DVDs and CDs for a small fee per item, and waives it for homebound patrons whose doctor fills out a certification form.

If your town is not listed, call your library and ask about homebound or outreach services.

Is there someone who will call or visit?

Friendly visiting and telephone reassurance programs match a volunteer with an older adult who lives alone or feels cut off. A few New Jersey examples:

  • Warren County runs Friendly Visitors and Callers for residents 60 and older who live alone, feel isolated, are frail, or are dealing with a move, a loss or health problems. When a visit is not a good fit, a volunteer calls instead.
  • Meals on Wheels in Greater New Brunswick has a Friendly Visitor program for homebound clients, with home visits, weekly phone calls, or cards and letters.
  • Some police departments run a daily check-in. In Waldwick, people 55 and older who live alone call police dispatch at a set time each day. If no call comes in, a dispatcher phones, and if there is still no answer, an officer stops by. It is free. Ask your own police department if it has something similar.

To find a program near you, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. It connects you to your county office on aging, which keeps track of visiting programs, senior centers and volunteer groups. Our guide to staying connected has more ideas, and if meals are part of the picture, see Meals on Wheels in New Jersey.

Can I take classes without leaving home?

You need a tablet, computer or smartphone, and a little patience the first time.

  • GetSetUp. New Jersey's Division of Aging Services lists free virtual classes taught by older adults through GetSetUp. Topics include cooking, fitness, music, photography, technology and travel. Start at getsetup.io/partner/NJ.
  • Senior Planet from AARP. Senior Planet offers online technology classes, and its free hotline at 1-888-713-3495 helps with tech questions Monday through Saturday in English, Spanish or Mandarin. If you need more help, you can set up a free one-on-one Zoom session with a volunteer.
  • Your senior center. Some town and county senior centers stream exercise classes, talks or games. Ask yours.

Want something more demanding, like a college-style course or a new language? Our guide to learning something new after 60 covers programs around the state.

What can I do at home to stay busy and happy?

The best activity is the one you look forward to. Some ideas that work well indoors or on a porch:

  • Music. Play records or a streaming station from your younger years, sing along, or pick up an instrument you played as a kid. A cheap keyboard or ukulele is a fine place to start.
  • Art and handwork. Watercolors, adult coloring books, knitting, crochet, quilting or scrapbooking old photos with a grandchild.
  • Puzzles and games. Jigsaw puzzles, crosswords, word searches and card games. Phone or video games with family count too.
  • Container gardening. A few pots of herbs, tomatoes or flowers on a sunny windowsill, porch or balcony give you something to tend every day. Raised planters save your knees and back.

Some services send a teacher or activity host to the home for lessons in music, art, yoga or games. Home Happenings, a service from this site's publisher, is launching soon to bring local teachers to homes in Essex County and nearby towns for music, art, yoga and games.

How can I exercise safely at home?

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults 65 and older aim for 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, muscle strengthening on at least two days, and balance activities. If health conditions make that hard, the CDC says to be as active as your abilities allow, and that some activity is better than none.

The National Institute on Aging (NIA) suggests simple moves you can do in a living room:

  • Strength: leg raises, pushups and squats, then resistance bands or hand weights once the movements feel easy.
  • Balance: standing on one foot, walking heel to toe, and practicing standing up from a chair, with a sturdy chair or wall nearby to hold.
  • Safety: breathe out during the effort, do not hold your breath, go slowly, and do not work the same muscles two days in a row.

Ask your doctor or physical therapist which exercises fit your health.

How do I get a ride for an occasional outing?

Staying home most days does not have to mean staying home every day.

ServiceWho it servesHow to start
County community transportationVaries by county. Many serve older adults and people with disabilities, often for medical trips, shopping and senior centersCall your county. NJ Transit lists each county's number on its Community Transportation page. Passaic County Paratransit: 973-305-5756
NJ Transit Access LinkPeople whose disability keeps them from using local buses or light railCall 973-491-4224, option 1, to start the eligibility process, which includes an interview and medical verification
NJ Transit buses and trainsRiders 62 and older pay a reduced fareSee our guide to NJ Transit senior fares

Access Link runs in the same areas and at the same hours as local buses, curb to curb. Fares are based on the local bus fare, and an approved personal care attendant rides free. Reduced fare cards are not accepted on Access Link. Book ahead, since rides are scheduled within a window around the time you ask for.

What are the signs of isolation?

The NIA links loneliness and social isolation to high blood pressure, heart disease, depression, cognitive decline and earlier death. Signs that someone may be cut off include:

  • Going days without talking to anyone
  • Losing interest in hobbies, meals or getting dressed
  • Sleeping much more or less than usual, or drinking more
  • Struggling with everyday tasks such as bills, medicines or cooking
  • Pulling back from conversations, which sometimes means hearing loss needs attention

Start with a call to the county office on aging at 1-877-222-3737 or the national Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116. Tell the doctor about low moods or a big change. If you or someone you love is in emotional distress, call or text 988, any time, for free. In an emergency, call 911. If you suspect neglect or abuse, see how to report elder abuse in New Jersey.

What can family members do?

A few steps help a lot. Set up a regular call at the same time each day or week. Sign your parent up for library delivery and a friendly caller. Put a tablet in their hands with large icons and favorite contacts already saved. Plan one outing a month and book the ride early. If memory loss is part of the picture, our guide to dementia support in New Jersey lists help, and if you are worn out, read about respite care for caregivers.

faq.q: How can a homebound senior in New Jersey get library books?
faq.a: Ask your local or county library about homebound delivery or books by mail. If reading print or holding a book is hard, the NJ State Library Talking Book and Braille Center mails audiobooks for free. Call 1-800-792-8322.

faq.q: Is there a program that calls older adults who live alone?
faq.a: Yes. Many counties, nonprofits and some police departments run telephone reassurance or friendly caller programs. Call 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging and ask what is available.

faq.q: What exercise can older adults do at home?
faq.a: The NIA suggests leg raises, pushups and squats for strength, and standing on one foot, walking heel to toe or practicing standing up from a chair for balance, with a sturdy chair or wall nearby. Check with your doctor first.

faq.q: How do I get a ride if I can't drive or take the bus?
faq.a: Call your county's community transportation service, which often serves older adults and people with disabilities. If a disability keeps you from using local buses, call NJ Transit Access Link at 973-491-4224, option 1, to apply.

title: Gift ideas for older parents and grandparents in NJ
dek: Theater nights, museum memberships, park passes, lessons at home and gifts of time. Holiday ideas for 2026 that favor experiences over more things to store.
keyFacts: NJ residents 62 and older may qualify for a Senior Citizen Pass that gives free entrance to state parks that charge fees.
NJ TRANSIT charges riders 62 and older half the regular one-way fare.
The Newark Museum of Art sells gift memberships with free admission all year.
The FTC says only scammers ask to be paid with gift cards.
body:
By the time most people reach their 70s or 80s, the house is full. Closets hold decades of sweaters, and the kitchen drawers are packed. What many older parents and grandparents would like more of is time out of the house, something to look forward to and a reason to see the people they love. This guide collects gift ideas for the 2026 holidays that lean toward experiences, with New Jersey examples we checked on each organization's own website.

The best experience gift is one they will actually use. Think about where they already like to go, how far they can comfortably travel and whether they would rather go alone, with a friend or with you. A good rule is to pair the gift with a plan. A theater gift card means more when it comes with a note that says "I'll drive, and we'll have lunch first."

Can I give a night at the theater?

Yes. Two of New Jersey's biggest stages sell gifts that the recipient can use for the show of their choice.

  • Paper Mill Playhouse in Millburn sells digital gift cards on its website (it says it can't offer physical cards right now). They can be used for tickets or for food and drinks in the theater's Carriage House Restaurant. Paper Mill's discounts page does not list a senior discount, so plan on regular prices.
  • NJPAC in Newark sells gift certificates online and at its box office. They can be used for performances, advance parking vouchers and memberships. Certificates are redeemed at the box office or by phone at 1-888-696-5722, not in online orders, and they can't be used for New Jersey Symphony tickets.

If hearing is a worry, Paper Mill lends assistive listening devices at its access services window in the lower lobby and schedules open-captioned and audio-described performances for every Mainstage show. It also has wheelchair seating with companion seats nearby. For other theaters, call the box office and ask what they offer before you buy.

Which New Jersey museums offer memberships?

A membership turns one visit into a year of easy outings. Members usually get in free every time, which takes the pressure off seeing everything in one trip.

MuseumWhat we found on its site
Newark Museum of ArtSells gift memberships from Individual to Family and higher levels, sent as a digital e-card. Members get unlimited free admission and reciprocal admission to more than 500 museums in the U.S. and Canada.
Montclair Art MuseumIndividual and Dual memberships carry a 10% discount for seniors 65 and older. The site does not describe a gift membership, so call to ask about buying one in someone else's name.
Morris Museum (Morristown)Has a Senior Citizen membership for ages 65 and up, with free admission all year and discounts at the Bickford Theatre and the Museum Shop. Ask the museum how to buy it as a gift.

Many local historical societies, arboretums and nature centers sell memberships too. A small, nearby place they will visit often can be a better fit than a famous one that is an hour away.

What does New Jersey offer seniors at state parks?

New Jersey residents age 62 or older, and residents with disabilities, may qualify for a Senior Citizen or Disability Pass. The state says it gives free entrance to parks that charge walk-in or parking fees and discounted camping rates. The NJ State Park Service notes that these passes are being updated, so check its park pass page for how to apply. If your parent is 62 or older, the gift might be helping them apply, then planning a spring walk or picnic together. Younger relatives can buy the regular annual State Park Pass, which covers parks that charge daily walk-in or parking fees for one calendar year.

Are classes a good gift?

They can be wonderful, especially for someone who has said "I always wanted to try that." Painting, a language, a cooking class or a lecture series gives a person a weekly reason to get out and meet people. Many senior centers, libraries, county colleges and museums run classes, and the Montclair Art Museum gives members a discount on art classes. Our guide to learning something new after 60 lists options around the state.

What if they don't drive anymore?

A gift of lessons that come to the house can suit someone who no longer drives or doesn't like going out in winter. A teacher can bring music, painting, chair yoga or a weekly game of cards or Scrabble to the kitchen table. Look for local teachers through your town's recreation department, a senior center or word of mouth. Home Happenings, a service from this site's publisher, is launching soon to bring local teachers to homes in Essex County and nearby towns for music, art, yoga and games.

Rides are a gift in themselves. You can offer a standing ride to a weekly activity, or set aside a few Saturdays for errands and outings. NJ TRANSIT charges riders 62 and older half the regular one-way fare (65 for trips to or from Metro-North stations on the Port Jervis Line). Bring an ID with your date of birth from a government, social service or transit agency, such as a Medicare card, driver's license or passport. A train trip into the city together can be its own outing.

What practical gifts make daily life easier?

  • Tech help. Set up a new phone or tablet, enlarge the text, add favorite contacts and write simple steps on a card. Then come back a week later to answer questions.
  • Easier phones and video calling. Large-button phones, simple tablets and tabletop video-calling screens let grandparents see the grandkids without fiddling with settings. Set it up before you wrap it.
  • Safety items. Grab bars, brighter lighting, night lights and non-slip mats can prevent a fall. Our aging in place guide covers what helps most and who can install it.
  • Meal delivery. A few weeks of prepared meals or a grocery delivery plan can be a relief after a hospital stay or for someone who has stopped enjoying cooking for one. Check that the menu fits any diet their doctor recommends.

What are some gifts of time?

For many grandparents, the gift they remember is the one that brought the family closer.

  • Recorded family stories. Sit down with a phone and ask about their first job, how they met, or the house they grew up in. Save the recordings and share them with the family.
  • A photo book. Scan old prints and mix them with new pictures of the grandchildren. Add names and dates while they can still tell you who everyone is.
  • A standing weekly call. Pick a day and time and stick to it. A promise of "every Sunday at 4" is something to look forward to all week.
  • Outings together. Write up a few coupons for trips you'll take in the new year. Our list of easy day trips in New Jersey has ideas in every region.

How do I choose the right gift?

  • Ask what they would use. It is fine to ask directly, or to ask a sibling or a friend of theirs.
  • Think about mobility and hearing. Stairs, long walks, parking and loud rooms can turn a nice idea into a hard day. Call ahead about seating, elevators and listening devices.
  • Avoid clutter. If they are downsizing, choose things that get used up or experienced.
  • Watch for gift card scams. The Federal Trade Commission says no real business or government agency will ever ask to be paid with a gift card. When you buy one, check that the packaging and PIN haven't been tampered with and keep the receipt. Our guide to scams targeting NJ seniors explains other common tricks.

Whatever you choose, the note you write with it may matter as much as the gift. Tell them why you picked it, and when you plan to share it with them.

faq.q: What is a good gift for an older parent who has everything?
faq.a: Choose an experience or your time: a theater outing, a museum membership, lessons, a photo book of family pictures or a standing weekly call. Pair it with a plan so it actually gets used.

faq.q: Do New Jersey seniors get into state parks free?
faq.a: New Jersey residents 62 and older, and residents with disabilities, may qualify for a Senior Citizen or Disability Pass that gives free entrance to parks that charge fees and discounted camping. The state says these passes are being updated, so check the NJ State Park Service park pass page to apply.

faq.q: Does Paper Mill Playhouse have a senior discount?
faq.a: Its discounts page does not list one. Paper Mill sells digital gift cards that can be used for tickets or at its Carriage House Restaurant, and it offers assistive listening devices and open-captioned performances.

faq.q: Is it safe to give a gift card to an older relative?
faq.a: Yes, if you buy it from a store you trust, check that the packaging and PIN are intact and keep the receipt. Remind them that no real business or government agency will ever ask to be paid with a gift card.
